newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to lift ban on offshore futures in April.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to lift ban on offshore futures in April.

text.p: Taiwan Finance Minister Paul Chiu said on Wednesday the island would lift a ban on local trading of offshore Taiwan stock-index futures in April.
"The Taiwan Stock Exchange will launch stock warrants in April before the offshore stock-index futures are approved, but both will be approved in April," Chiu told reporters.
Chiu's comment put to rest lingering uncertainty over when or even if Taiwan would legalise access by local investors to offshore futures linked to Taiwan's stock market performance.
Such contracts were launched on January 9 by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and Singapore International Monetary Exchange over the objections of Taiwan's market regulators.

Earlier on Wednesday in comments to parliament, Chiu had voiced support for ending the ban and said he would announce a decision by the end of April. But he stopped short of saying explicitly that a liberalisation was in the works.
"We will decide on the trading of offshore stock-index futures by the end of April," Chiu said. "The finance ministry is leaning toward allowing it. We have a positive attitude."
Chiu issued the subsequent confirmation when pressed by reporters to clarify his earlier remarks.

Under the liberalisation, Taiwan futures houses will be allowed to trade the SIMEX and CME futures on behalf of local Taiwan investors, some of whom are believed to have been evading the ban by placing orders through offshore brokers.
The launch of the offshore contracts had created enormous pressure on Taiwan to speed up establishment of its own futures exchange and to legalise trading of the CME and SIMEX futures.

Similarly, the introduction of Taiwan's first domestic stock warrants comes in the face of intense competition in overseas markets, where warrants on Taiwan stocks issued by financial institutions have been growing in popularity.
Taiwan brokerages have not been allowed to offer the overseas warrants, but local investors are known to have traded them through offshore accounts.
